```{r cds-cmip6-sst-download}
#| label: cds-cmip6-sst-download
#| cache: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false

# ── Download CMIP6 sea surface temperature (tos) from Copernicus CDS ──────────
# Ten coupled ScenarioMIP models with tos available for all three SSPs.
# Monthly resolution, spatially subsetted to a 3° box around Moorea LTER Site 1
# (-17.48°S, -149.83°W). Four experiments: historical (1950-2014) +
# SSP1-2.6 / SSP2-4.5 / SSP5-8.5 (2015-2100).
# Note: CDS processes requests server-side; first run may take 30–90 minutes.

library(ecmwfr)

dir.create("data/cmip6_sst", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

cmip6_models <- c(
  "access_cm2", "bcc_csm2_mr", "ec_earth3",
  "gfdl_esm4",  "ipsl_cm6a_lr", "miroc6",
  "mpi_esm1_2_lr", "mri_esm2_0", "noresm2_lm", "ukesm1_0_ll"
)

# Bounding box: N, W, S, E (degrees, -180 to 180)
moorea_area <- c(-16.0, -151.0, -19.0, -148.0)

all_months <- as.list(sprintf("%02d", 1:12))

build_sst_request <- function(experiment, years, target_file) {
  list(
    dataset_short_name  = "projections-cmip6",
    temporal_resolution = "monthly",
    experiment          = experiment,
    variable            = "sea_surface_temperature",
    model               = as.list(cmip6_models),
    year                = as.list(as.character(years)),
    month               = all_months,
    area                = moorea_area,
    target              = target_file
  )
}

requests <- list(
  build_sst_request("historical", 1950:2014, "tos_historical.zip"),
  build_sst_request("ssp1_2_6",  2015:2100, "tos_ssp126.zip"),
  build_sst_request("ssp2_4_5",  2015:2100, "tos_ssp245.zip"),
  build_sst_request("ssp5_8_5",  2015:2100, "tos_ssp585.zip")
)

wf_request_batch(requests, workers = 2, path = "data/cmip6_sst/")
```

```{r cds-cmip6-sst-process}
#| label: cds-cmip6-sst-process
#| cache: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false

# ── Read CDS NetCDF files, extract Moorea grid cell, bias-correct ─────────────
# Produces:
#   wb_proj_bc   — ensemble p10/median/p90 per scenario-year (used in propagation)
#   ann_cmip6_bc — per-model historical annual max SST (used for spread ribbon)

library(ncdf4)

sst_dir    <- "data/cmip6_sst"
moorea_lon <- -149.83
moorea_lat <- -17.48

# Extract model name from CMIP6 standard filename:
# <var>_<freq>_<model>_<exp>_<variant>_<grid>_<period>.nc
extract_model_name <- function(filepath) {
  parts <- strsplit(basename(filepath), "_")[[1]]
  if (length(parts) >= 3) parts[3] else "unknown"
}

read_tos_nc <- function(nc_path, experiment) {
  nc <- nc_open(nc_path)
  on.exit(nc_close(nc))

  model <- extract_model_name(nc_path)

  # Coordinates — handle both 1-D regular and 2-D curvilinear grids
  lon <- tryCatch(ncvar_get(nc, "lon"), error = \(e) ncvar_get(nc, "longitude"))
  lat <- tryCatch(ncvar_get(nc, "lat"), error = \(e) ncvar_get(nc, "latitude"))

  # Normalise 0–360 longitudes to -180–180
  lon_norm <- ifelse(lon > 180, lon - 360, lon)

  if (length(dim(lon)) == 2) {
    # Curvilinear grid
    dist  <- sqrt((lon_norm - moorea_lon)^2 + (lat - moorea_lat)^2)
    idx   <- which(dist == min(dist, na.rm = TRUE), arr.ind = TRUE)
    tos_raw <- ncvar_get(nc, "tos")[idx[1, 1], idx[1, 2], ]
  } else {
    i_lon   <- which.min(abs(lon_norm - moorea_lon))
    i_lat   <- which.min(abs(lat      - moorea_lat))
    tos_raw <- ncvar_get(nc, "tos")[i_lon, i_lat, ]
  }

  # Time → calendar dates
  time_raw   <- ncvar_get(nc, "time")
  time_units <- ncatt_get(nc, "time", "units")$value
  origin_str <- sub("^days since ", "", time_units)
  dates      <- as.Date(origin_str) + as.integer(round(time_raw))

  # Replace fill values with NA
  fv <- ncatt_get(nc, "tos", "_FillValue")$value
  if (length(fv) > 0) tos_raw[abs(tos_raw - fv) < abs(fv) * 1e-3] <- NA

  # Convert Kelvin → Celsius if needed
  u <- ncatt_get(nc, "tos", "units")$value
  if (length(u) > 0 && grepl("^K$|kelvin", u, ignore.case = TRUE))
    tos_raw <- tos_raw - 273.15

  n <- min(length(dates), length(tos_raw))
  tibble(model      = model,
         experiment = experiment,
         date       = dates[seq_len(n)],
         tos        = as.numeric(tos_raw[seq_len(n)]))
}

zip_meta <- tibble(
  zip_file   = file.path(sst_dir, c("tos_historical.zip", "tos_ssp126.zip",
                                     "tos_ssp245.zip",    "tos_ssp585.zip")),
  experiment = c("historical", "ssp1_2_6", "ssp2_4_5", "ssp5_8_5")
)

all_tos <- pmap_dfr(zip_meta, function(zip_file, experiment) {
  if (!file.exists(zip_file)) { warning("Missing: ", zip_file); return(NULL) }
  td <- file.path(sst_dir, experiment)
  dir.create(td, showWarnings = FALSE)
  unzip(zip_file, exdir = td, overwrite = FALSE)
  nc_files <- list.files(td, pattern = "\\.nc$", full.names = TRUE)
  map_dfr(nc_files, \(f) tryCatch(
    read_tos_nc(f, experiment),
    error = \(e) { warning(basename(f), ": ", e$message); NULL }
  ))
})

# Annual maximum SST per model-year
ann_tos <- all_tos |>
  mutate(year = year(date)) |>
  group_by(model, experiment, year) |>
  summarise(ann_max = max(tos, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(is.finite(ann_max))

# ── Delta bias correction: anchor each model to observed MCR 2005-2025 mean ───
obs_mean_mcr_cds <- mean(Year_Averages$Max_temp[Year_Averages$Year %in% 2005:2025],
                         na.rm = TRUE)

bias_tbl_cds <- ann_tos |>
  filter(
    (experiment == "historical"                            & year %in% 2005:2014) |
    (experiment %in% c("ssp1_2_6","ssp2_4_5","ssp5_8_5") & year %in% 2015:2025)
  ) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(model_mean = mean(ann_max, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(bias = obs_mean_mcr_cds - model_mean)

ann_tos_bc <- ann_tos |>
  left_join(bias_tbl_cds, by = "model") |>
  mutate(ann_max_bc = ann_max + bias)

# ── Ensemble p10 / median / p90 per experiment-year ───────────────────────────
ens_stats <- function(data, exp_name) {
  data |>
    filter(experiment == exp_name) |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(p10    = quantile(ann_max_bc, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE),
              median = quantile(ann_max_bc, 0.50, na.rm = TRUE),
              p90    = quantile(ann_max_bc, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(experiment = exp_name)
}

ssp_ens  <- bind_rows(
  ens_stats(ann_tos_bc, "ssp1_2_6"),
  ens_stats(ann_tos_bc, "ssp2_4_5"),
  ens_stats(ann_tos_bc, "ssp5_8_5")
)
hist_ens <- ens_stats(ann_tos_bc, "historical")

# ── Build wb_proj_bc (structure expected by downstream propagation code) ───────
ssp_long <- ssp_ens |>
  pivot_longer(c(p10, median, p90), names_to = "percentile", values_to = "tasmax_bc") |>
  mutate(scenario = case_when(
    experiment == "ssp1_2_6" ~ "ssp126",
    experiment == "ssp2_4_5" ~ "ssp245",
    experiment == "ssp5_8_5" ~ "ssp585"
  )) |>
  select(year, scenario, percentile, tasmax_bc)

# Historical 2005-2014 expanded across all three scenarios for the overlap window
hist_long <- hist_ens |>
  filter(year %in% 2005:2014) |>
  pivot_longer(c(p10, median, p90), names_to = "percentile", values_to = "tasmax_bc") |>
  select(year, percentile, tasmax_bc) |>
  expand_grid(scenario = c("ssp126", "ssp245", "ssp585"))

wb_proj_bc <- bind_rows(hist_long, ssp_long) |>
  distinct(year, scenario, percentile, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  arrange(scenario, percentile, year) |>
  filter(year %in% 2005:2100)

# ── ann_cmip6_bc: historical per-model series for the 2005-2014 spread ribbon ─
ann_cmip6_bc <- ann_tos_bc |>
  filter(experiment == "historical")
```

```{r wb-cmip6-propagate}
#| label: wb-cmip6-propagate

# ── Propagate each SSP scenario × CMIP6 percentile through the reduced SEM ───
propagate_wb_ssp <- function(scenario_name, pct = "median") {
  temps_bc <- wb_proj_bc |>
    filter(scenario == scenario_name, percentile == pct) |>
    arrange(year) |>
    pull(tasmax_bc)

  temp_z <- (temps_bc - modelmean$temperature) / modelsd$temperature
  tm     <- matrix(rep(temp_z, each = n_r), nrow = n_r)

  yr_rv <- sapply(2005:2100, function(y) {
    row <- yr_resid_lookup |> filter(Year == y)
    if (nrow(row) == 1 && !is.na(row$yr)) row$yr else 0
  })
  yrm <- matrix(rep(yr_rv, each = n_r), nrow = n_r)

  cm <- pmin(rs(post_r$b_logcoral_temperature, tm) +
             rs(post_r$b_logcoral_yearresid,   yrm) + post_r$b_logcoral_Intercept, z_ceil_coral)
  rm <- rs(post_r$b_logrd_logcoral, cm)         + post_r$b_logrd_Intercept
  fm <- pmin(rs(post_r$b_logfleshy_logcoral, cm) + post_r$b_logfleshy_Intercept, z_ceil_fleshy)
  pm <- rs(post_r$bsp_logpmax_milogrd, rm)      + post_r$b_logpmax_Intercept
  nm <- rs(post_r$bsp_Npercent_milogrd, rm)     + post_r$b_Npercent_Intercept

  imap_dfr(
    list(Temperature    = bt_lin(tm, modelmean$temperature, modelsd$temperature),
         `Coral Cover`  = bt_log(cm, modelmean$logcoral,   modelsd$logcoral),
         Respiration    = bt_log(rm, modelmean$logrd,      modelsd$logrd),
         `Fleshy Algae` = bt_log(fm, modelmean$logfleshy,  modelsd$logfleshy),
         Pmax           = bt_log(pm, modelmean$logpmax,    modelsd$logpmax),
         `N Content`    = bt_log(nm,
                                 mean(log(Year_Averages$N_percent), na.rm = TRUE),
                                 sd(log(Year_Averages$N_percent),   na.rm = TRUE))),
    function(mat, vname) {
      tibble(scenario = scenario_name, percentile = pct, variable = vname,
             year = rep(2005:2100, each = n_r), value = as.vector(mat)) |>
        group_by(scenario, percentile, variable, year) |>
        summarise(median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
                  lo95 = quantile(value, .025, na.rm = TRUE),
                  hi95 = quantile(value, .975, na.rm = TRUE),
                  lo50 = quantile(value, .25,  na.rm = TRUE),
                  hi50 = quantile(value, .75,  na.rm = TRUE),
                  .groups = "drop")
    })
}

wb_all_combos <- expand_grid(
  scenario   = c("ssp126", "ssp245", "ssp585"),
  percentile = c("p10", "median", "p90")
)
wb_proj_tbl <- bind_rows(
  mapply(propagate_wb_ssp,
         scenario_name = wb_all_combos$scenario,
         pct           = wb_all_combos$percentile,
         SIMPLIFY      = FALSE)
)

# ── Tidy for plotting ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
wb_sem_ci_band <- wb_proj_tbl |>
  filter(percentile == "median") |>
  select(scenario, variable, year, central = median, lo_sem = lo95, hi_sem = hi95)

wb_clim_band <- wb_proj_tbl |>
  filter(percentile %in% c("p10", "p90")) |>
  select(scenario, variable, year, percentile, clim_med = median) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = percentile, values_from = clim_med) |>
  rename(lo_clim = p10, hi_clim = p90)

wb_ssp_labels  <- c(ssp126 = "SSP1-2.6", ssp245 = "SSP2-4.5", ssp585 = "SSP5-8.5")
wb_ssp_colours <- c(ssp126 = "#2196F3",  ssp245 = "#FF9800",   ssp585 = "#E53935")
wb_var_order   <- c("Temperature","Coral Cover","Respiration",
                    "Fleshy Algae","Pmax","N Content")
wb_var_units   <- c(Temperature    = "\u00b0C",
                    `Coral Cover`  = "% cover",
                    Respiration    = "mmol O\u2082 m\u207b\u00b2 hr\u207b\u00b9",
                    `Fleshy Algae` = "% cover",
                    Pmax           = "mmol O\u2082 m\u207b\u00b2 hr\u207b\u00b9",
                    `N Content`    = "% N")

wb_plot_tbl <- wb_sem_ci_band |>
  left_join(wb_clim_band, by = c("scenario", "variable", "year")) |>
  mutate(variable       = factor(variable, levels = wb_var_order),
         scenario_label = wb_ssp_labels[scenario])

# ── Patch: historical temperature spread from Open-Meteo 7-model ensemble ─────
# The WorldBank historical series has no p10/p90; substitute the inter-model
# spread (p10–p90 across 7 bias-corrected HighResMIP models) for 2005–2014.
om_hist_spread <- ann_cmip6_bc |>
  filter(year %in% 2005:2014) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(lo_clim_om = quantile(ann_max_bc, 0.10),
            hi_clim_om = quantile(ann_max_bc, 0.90),
            .groups = "drop")

wb_plot_tbl <- wb_plot_tbl |>
  left_join(om_hist_spread, by = "year") |>
  mutate(
    lo_clim = if_else(variable == "Temperature" & year %in% 2005:2014,
                      lo_clim_om, lo_clim),
    hi_clim = if_else(variable == "Temperature" & year %in% 2005:2014,
                      hi_clim_om, hi_clim)
  ) |>
  select(-lo_clim_om, -hi_clim_om)
```

```{r fig-wb-cmip6}
#| label: fig-wb-cmip6
#| fig-cap: "**CMIP6 SST multi-scenario projections for MCR LTER Site 1 backreef, 2005–2100.** Annual maximum sea surface temperature (*tos*) was obtained from ten coupled CMIP6 ScenarioMIP models (ACCESS-CM2, BCC-CSM2-MR, EC-Earth3, GFDL-ESM4, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MIROC6, MPI-ESM1-2-LR, MRI-ESM2-0, NorESM2-LM, UKESM1-0-LL) downloaded from the Copernicus Climate Data Store for the Moorea grid cell (~17.5°S, 149.8°W) under three shared socioeconomic pathways: SSP1-2.6 (blue), SSP2-4.5 (orange), and SSP5-8.5 (red), for 2015–2100, stitched to the historical CMIP6 run (1950–2014). Each model was delta bias-corrected to the 2005–2025 MCR observational mean (additive shift per model) before computing the ensemble p10, median, and p90. Bias-corrected temperatures were z-scored and propagated through the fitted reduced Bayesian SEM. Inner ribbons: 95% credible interval from the SEM posterior (3,000 draws; CMIP6 ensemble median SST). Outer ribbons (temperature panel): CMIP6 multi-model p10–p90 spread. Open circles: observed 2005–2025 values. Grey shading: forecast period. Fleshy algae y-axis capped at 100% cover (the log-linear SEM projects >100% under SSP5-8.5, which is biologically impossible and reflects model extrapolation beyond observed range)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8

wb_y_limits <- list(
  Temperature    = NULL,
  `Coral Cover`  = c(0, NA),
  Respiration    = c(0, NA),
  `Fleshy Algae` = c(0, 100),
  Pmax           = c(60, NA),
  `N Content`    = c(0.3, NA)
)

make_wb_panel <- function(vname) {
  d_v   <- wb_plot_tbl |> filter(variable == vname)
  obs_v <- Year_Averages |>
    select(year = Year,
           Temperature    = Max_temp,
           `Coral Cover`  = mean_coral,
           Respiration    = Rd,
           `Fleshy Algae` = mean_fleshy,
           Pmax           = Pmax,
           `N Content`    = N_percent) |>
    pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "variable", values_to = "obs") |>
    filter(variable == vname)
  unit <- wb_var_units[[vname]]
  ylim <- wb_y_limits[[vname]]

  p <- ggplot(d_v, aes(x = year, colour = scenario, fill = scenario)) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = 2025.5, xmax = 2100, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
             fill = "grey92", alpha = .6) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo_clim, ymax = hi_clim), alpha = 0.10, colour = NA) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo_sem,  ymax = hi_sem),  alpha = 0.20, colour = NA) +
    geom_line(aes(y = central), linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(data = obs_v, aes(x = year, y = obs),
               colour = "black", size = 1.5, shape = 21, fill = "white",
               inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 2025.5, linetype = "dashed",
               colour = "grey50", linewidth = .4) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = wb_ssp_colours, labels = wb_ssp_labels, name = "Scenario") +
    scale_fill_manual(  values = wb_ssp_colours, labels = wb_ssp_labels, name = "Scenario") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2010, 2100, 20)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = unit, title = vname) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
    theme(legend.position = "none",
          plot.title = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold"),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
  if (!is.null(ylim)) p <- p + coord_cartesian(ylim = ylim)
  if (vname == "Fleshy Algae")
    p <- p + annotate("text", x = 2060, y = 96,
                      label = "100% ceiling", size = 2.3, colour = "grey40",
                      hjust = 0.5, fontface = "italic")
  p
}

wb_panels <- lapply(wb_var_order, make_wb_panel)

wb_legend_plot <- ggplot(
  wb_plot_tbl |> filter(variable == "Temperature"),
  aes(x = year, y = central, colour = scenario, fill = scenario)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo_sem, ymax = hi_sem), alpha = .25, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = wb_ssp_colours, labels = wb_ssp_labels,
                      name = "CMIP6 Scenario") +
  scale_fill_manual(  values = wb_ssp_colours, labels = wb_ssp_labels,
                      name = "CMIP6 Scenario") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(linewidth = 1.5))) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "right", legend.direction = "vertical",
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8.5, face = "bold"),
        legend.text  = element_text(size = 8))
wb_leg <- cowplot::get_legend(wb_legend_plot)

wb_main <- wrap_plots(wb_panels, ncol = 2) & theme(legend.position = "none")
cowplot::plot_grid(wb_main, wb_leg, ncol = 2, rel_widths = c(1, 0.12))
```

```{r tbl-wb-cmip6}
#| label: tbl-wb-cmip6
#| tbl-cap: "CMIP6 SST ensemble projections at 2050, 2075, and 2100 under three SSP scenarios (reduced SEM, CMIP6 ensemble median SST). Values are posterior median (95% credible interval). Temperature CIs are negligible because the SEM does not add uncertainty to the input forcing. Fleshy Algae values >100% under SSP5-8.5 reflect log-linear model extrapolation beyond biological limits."

wb_tbl_out <- bind_rows(lapply(c(2050, 2075, 2100), function(yr) {
  wb_proj_tbl |>
    filter(percentile == "median", year == yr) |>
    mutate(scenario_label = wb_ssp_labels[scenario],
           label = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f\u2013%.1f)", median, lo95, hi95)) |>
    select(variable, scenario_label, label) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = scenario_label, values_from = label) |>
    mutate(Year = yr) |>
    relocate(Year, variable)
})) |>
  arrange(variable, Year) |>
  rename(Variable = variable)

knitr::kable(wb_tbl_out, align = c("r","l","c","c","c"))
```

### Results: CMIP6 SST projections to 2100

Extending the CMIP6 SST forcing to 2100 using a ten-model coupled ensemble from the Copernicus CDS under three SSPs reveals strong scenario dependence across all ecosystem variables (Fig. @fig-wb-cmip6, Table @tbl-wb-cmip6). By 2050, scenario differences are modest (coral cover: SSP1-2.6 5.8% vs. SSP5-8.5 4.2%), consistent with the narrow divergence between scenarios before mid-century. Post-2050, trajectories diverge sharply, particularly under SSP5-8.5.

Under **SSP1-2.6** (aggressive mitigation), temperature stabilises near 30°C after mid-century, and coral cover stabilises at approximately 6% — near current (2025) levels — with no further long-term decline. Ecosystem respiration remains relatively stable at ~33 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹, and fleshy algae stays bounded around 20–25% cover.

Under **SSP5-8.5** (high-emissions), temperature reaches ~32°C by 2100, driving coral cover to 0.9% (95% CI: 0.3–2.8%) — effectively near-complete loss. Ecosystem respiration collapses to 16.6 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ (−71% from 2005 levels), and fleshy macroalgae expands beyond the 100% biological ceiling in the model's log-linear extrapolation, indicating a complete phase shift to algae dominance. The scenario contrast in coral cover at 2100 is approximately **7-fold** (6.2% vs. 0.9%), illustrating the substantial leverage of emissions trajectory on reef state.

**SSP2-4.5** projects an intermediate outcome, with coral reaching 3.5% by 2100, respiration at 27.2 mmol, and fleshy algae ~39%, comparable to the linear-trend projection for 2050.

Two caveats apply. First, the CMIP6 SST forcing is from coupled global models at ~1° resolution; the delta bias correction anchors each model's mean to the MCR observational record but cannot capture local oceanographic variability such as ENSO-driven anomalies or upwelling. Second, the log-linear SEM projects fleshy algae beyond physical limits (>100% cover) under extreme warming, an artefact of extrapolation beyond the observed range; these values should be interpreted as indicating a phase-shifted, algae-dominated state rather than literal cover percentages.

# Results & Interpretation

## Results

### Community composition and environmental change

The MCR LTER Site 1 backreef underwent substantial reorganisation over 2006–2025 (Fig. @fig-benthic). Coral cover declined from 31.0% to 6.8% (−78%), while fleshy macroalgae increased from 5.5% to 14.7% (+167%). Bayesian temporal trend models confirmed directional change across all major community variables (Fig. @fig-temporal): coral cover showed the strongest rate of decline (β = −0.14 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.70), corallivore fish biomass declined in parallel (β = −0.13 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.52), and herbivore biomass increased (β = +0.15 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.66). Annual maximum temperature increased modestly but consistently over the study period (β = +0.07 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.19), corresponding to approximately +0.65°C over 20 years. Algal tissue nitrogen content showed the strongest temporal signal among biogeochemical variables (β = −0.17 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.78).

### Ecosystem metabolism

Ecosystem respiration (Rd) declined markedly from a mean of 57 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ in 2008–2010 to 29 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ in 2021–2025 (−49%; β = −0.14 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.50). Maximum photosynthetic capacity (Pmax) also declined, from 124 to 105 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ between early and late periods (β = −0.08 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.19), though with weaker temporal signal. Net ecosystem production showed no significant directional trend (β = +0.08 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.20). These parameters were extracted from a Bayesian photosynthesis-irradiance (PI) curve model fit across 2,928 production measurements, with all chain convergence diagnostics satisfactory (Rhat < 1.01, ESS > 1,000 for all parameters).

### Causal pathways through the reef ecosystem

A Bayesian SEM encompassing eight response variables and 12 causal pathways revealed coral cover as the central mediator of ecosystem change (Fig. @fig-sem-dag, @fig-sem-conditional). Year was positively associated with temperature (β = 0.47, 95% CI 0.12–0.82), and temperature negatively drove coral cover (β = −0.55, 95% CI −0.83 to −0.28). A non-thermal temporal component — the residual of calendar year after removing the temperature trend — also credibly predicted coral cover (β = −0.67, 95% CI −0.93 to −0.41), capturing secular decline in coral cover unexplained by warming alone. Coral cover in turn was the strongest predictor of ecosystem respiration (β = 1.08, 95% CI 0.64–1.53), fleshy macroalgae (β = −0.91, 95% CI −1.13 to −0.70), and corallivore fish biomass (β = 0.65, 95% CI 0.26–1.02). Herbivore fish biomass was positively predicted by fleshy macroalgae cover (β = 0.71, 95% CI 0.37–1.06), consistent with bottom-up trophic control. Ecosystem respiration in turn predicted algal nitrogen content (β = 0.62, 95% CI 0.24–1.01) and Pmax (β = 0.82, 95% CI 0.03–1.62). Three tested pathways — direct temperature effects on respiration (β = 0.22, 95% CI −0.22 to 0.62) and Pmax (β = −0.16, 95% CI −0.78 to 0.45), and a direct coral effect on Pmax (β = −0.35, 95% CI −1.40 to 0.71) — had credible intervals that included zero. Bayesian R² was 0.22 for temperature and 0.71 for coral cover (the year-residual predictor accounted for the large improvement from the prior R² of 0.29).

### Temperature effects are predominantly indirect

Decomposing total temperature effects into direct and coral-mediated indirect pathways (Fig. @fig-temp-effects) revealed that coral decline was the dominant transmission mechanism for most ecosystem responses. The indirect effect of temperature on ecosystem respiration, operating through coral loss, was substantial and directionally credible (β_indirect = −0.58, 95% CI −1.01 to −0.25), while the direct thermal effect was inconclusive (β_direct = 0.22, 95% CI −0.22 to 0.62), and the total effect did not exclude zero (β_total = −0.38, 95% CI −0.85 to 0.08). For Pmax, direct and indirect pathways partially cancelled and neither was significant (β_total = 0.03, 95% CI −0.54 to 0.64). All indirect temperature effects on fleshy macroalgae (β = +0.50, 95% CI 0.25–0.79), corallivore fish (β = −0.34, 95% CI −0.66 to −0.11), herbivore fish (β = +0.35, 95% CI 0.14–0.66), and algal nitrogen content (β = −0.35, 95% CI −0.76 to −0.10) were mediated entirely through coral cover and had credible intervals excluding zero.

### Ecosystem projections under CMIP6 climate scenarios

Extending the SEM causal framework to 2100 using WorldBank CMIP6 temperature forcing under three SSP emission scenarios reveals strong dependence of reef ecosystem state on the trajectory of global emissions (Fig. @fig-wb-cmip6, Table @tbl-wb-cmip6).

**Near-term (to 2050).** Scenarios diverge only modestly before mid-century, consistent with similar temperature trajectories across SSPs prior to ~2040. Coral cover at 2050 is projected at 5.8% under SSP1-2.6 versus 4.2% under SSP5-8.5 — a relatively small contrast reflecting that near-term warming is largely committed regardless of emission pathway. Ecosystem respiration, fleshy macroalgae, Pmax, and N content show similarly narrow scenario separation at 2050.

**Mid-century (2050–2075).** Trajectories diverge sharply as scenario-dependent warming accumulates. Under SSP5-8.5, temperatures approach ~31°C by 2075, driving coral cover below 2% and ecosystem respiration below 22 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹. Under SSP1-2.6, temperatures stabilise near 30–30.5°C following the emissions peak, and coral cover remains above 5%. SSP2-4.5 follows an intermediate trajectory, with coral declining slowly toward 4%.

**End of century (2100).** The scenario contrast at 2100 is striking. Under SSP1-2.6, coral cover stabilises at 6.2% (posterior 95% CI: 2.4–14.3%), broadly near its 2025 level, while ecosystem respiration remains at 33 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ and fleshy macroalgae is held around 21% cover — a reef that is structurally degraded relative to 2005, but functionally persistent. Under SSP5-8.5, coral cover collapses to 0.9% (95% CI: 0.3–2.8%) — a 7-fold difference relative to SSP1-2.6. Ecosystem respiration falls to 16.6 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ (−71% relative to 2005 levels), and the fleshy macroalgae model extrapolates beyond the 100% biological ceiling, indicating an algae-dominated phase-shifted state. SSP2-4.5 projects an intermediate outcome: coral ~3.5% by 2100, respiration ~27 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹, and fleshy algae ~39% — comparable to the linear-trend projection for 2050, illustrating that intermediate emissions postpone but do not prevent continued reef degradation.

The ~2040–2060 window represents the critical divergence point, after which emission pathways commit the system to qualitatively different futures. The 7-fold contrast in coral cover at 2100 between SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 quantifies the ecological leverage of global emissions mitigation for reef persistence. Two caveats apply to these projections. First, the coupled-model SST forcing is at CMIP6 resolution (~1°); the delta bias correction captures the ensemble warming rate but not local oceanographic variability (e.g., ENSO anomalies, upwelling around Moorea). Second, the log-linear SEM extrapolates fleshy macroalgae beyond biological limits under SSP5-8.5, which should be interpreted as indicating a phase-shifted, algae-dominated state rather than literal cover percentages.

# Discussion



- **One Tree Island, Great Barrier Reef** (Kinsey 1985; Barnes 1983): 7-year study (1975-1982) using slack-water technique, documented mean gross production of 180-250 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ and net production near metabolic balance (slight net autotrophy). No long-term trend analysis due to relatively stable coral community during study period. Established baseline metabolic rates for healthy Indo-Pacific reef flats.

- **Kaneohe Bay, Hawaii** (Shamberger et al. 2011; Drupp et al. 2013): 5-year lagoon-scale study (2008-2013) combining in situ sensors with hydrodynamic modeling, reported net heterotrophy (-20 to -40 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹) in a degraded, eutrophic system. Demonstrated metabolic depression relative to historical baselines, attributed to sewage diversion recovery and persistent macroalgal dominance. Our MCR backreef shows similar net production decline but from initially higher autotrophy.

- **Heron Island, Great Barrier Reef** (McMahon et al. 2013; Santos et al. 2011): 3-year reef flat study (2009-2012) using Eulerian flow-through approach, documented seasonal cycles in metabolism with mean gross production ~150 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹. No significant interannual trends detected, though study period preceded major bleaching events. Shorter temporal extent limits comparison to multi-decadal dynamics.

- **Lady Elliot Island, Great Barrier Reef** (Shaw et al. 2015, 2018): 7-year record (2010-2017) using CO₂ and O₂ sensors, reported declining net community calcification (-50% over study period) correlated with bleaching events, but primary production metrics showed high seasonal/interannual variability without clear trends. Focused primarily on calcification rather than photosynthesis-respiration balance.

- **Bermuda reef platforms** (Yeakel et al. 2015; Courtney et al. 2016, 2018): Decadal-scale calcification records (1996-2015) from multiple platforms showing 40-50% decline in net calcification, strongly correlated with ocean acidification and warming. Limited concurrent primary production measurements, though inferred metabolic stress from calcification:production ratios.

- **Puerto Morelos, Mexican Caribbean** (Salinas-de-León et al. 2018): 4-year study (2012-2016) documenting metabolism across reef zones, found forereef remained autotrophic (NP ~20-40 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹) while backreef shifted toward heterotrophy following Hurricane Patricia. Demonstrated disturbance impacts on metabolism but limited baseline pre-disturbance data.

**Comparison to MCR backreef (this study)**: Our 20-year continuous record (2005-2025) represents one of the longest integrated metabolism time series globally for any coral reef habitat. Unlike most prior studies focused on calcification or snapshot metabolism measurements, we track simultaneous changes in gross production (via Pmax), ecosystem respiration (Rd), and net production alongside community composition and biogeochemistry.

```{r comparative-table}
#| label: tbl-comparative-metabolism
#| tbl-cap: "Comparative reef metabolism measurements from long-term studies"

# Create comparative table
comparative_metabolism <- tibble(
  Location = c("One Tree Island, GBR", "Kaneohe Bay, Hawaii", "Heron Island, GBR", 
               "Lady Elliot Island, GBR", "Puerto Morelos, Mexico", "MCR LTER Site 1 (This Study)"),
  Years = c("1975-1982", "2008-2013", "2009-2012", "2010-2017", "2012-2016", "2005-2025"),
  Duration = c("7 years", "5 years", "3 years", "7 years", "4 years", "20 years"),
  `Gross Production` = c("180-250", "Not reported", "~150", "Not reported", "Not reported", 
                        sprintf("%.0f-%.0f", 
                                min(Year_Averages$Pmax, na.rm = TRUE),
                                max(Year_Averages$Pmax, na.rm = TRUE))),
  `Net Production` = c("~0 (balanced)", "-20 to -40", "Variable", "Not primary focus", 
                      "20-40 (forereef)", 
                      sprintf("%.0f to %.0f",
                              min(Year_Averages$NP_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
                              max(Year_Averages$NP_mean, na.rm = TRUE))),
  `Metabolic State` = c("Balanced", "Heterotrophic", "Balanced/Variable", "Declining calcif.", 
                       "Autotrophic", "Autotroph→Balanced"),
  `Trend Detected` = c("No (stable)", "Yes (degraded)", "No (short)", "Yes (calcif.)", 
                      "Yes (disturbance)", "Yes (strong decline)")
)

knitr::kable(comparative_metabolism, 
             caption = "Comparative reef ecosystem metabolism from long-term studies. All gross and net production values in mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹. MCR LTER represents the longest continuous integrated metabolism record.",
             align = "lcccccc")
```

**Table Interpretation**: The MCR backreef shows gross production values (Pmax range `r sprintf("%.0f-%.0f", min(Year_Averages$Pmax, na.rm = TRUE), max(Year_Averages$Pmax, na.rm = TRUE))` mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹) comparable to other Indo-Pacific reefs like One Tree Island and Heron Island in their healthy state, but with a clear declining trajectory. Unlike the stable conditions at One Tree Island (1975-1982) or the acute degradation at Kaneohe Bay (eutrophication-driven), MCR represents a gradual climate-driven transition captured over an unprecedented 20-year period. The shift from net autotrophy toward metabolic balance parallels trends observed globally but with much finer temporal resolution.

Key distinctions from previous work:
1. **Temporal extent**: 20 years spans multiple disturbance events (bleaching, cyclones, crown-of-thorns outbreaks), enabling trend detection beyond interannual variability
2. **Mechanistic parameters**: Extraction of light-independent Pmax and Rd from PI curves provides physiological indices not captured by ambient flux measurements alone
3. **Integration**: Concurrent benthic surveys, fish censuses, and nutrient monitoring enable causal pathway analysis rather than correlative observations
4. **Directional trends**: Clear declines in both Pmax (~30% reduction) and Rd (~40% reduction) parallel coral loss, contrasting with stable or cyclical patterns in shorter time series from less impacted reefs
5. **Metabolic mode shift**: Initial net autotrophy (NP ~10-20 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹) transitioning toward metabolic balance, similar magnitude to Kaneohe Bay degradation but from different starting state and drivers (temperature vs. eutrophication)

Our results suggest that even reefs maintaining some coral cover experience functional degradation - metabolic capacity declines may precede dramatic compositional collapse, providing early warning of ecosystem dysfunction. The MCR backreef trajectory mirrors calcification declines observed in Bermuda and Lady Elliot Island but extends to the full production-respiration system, revealing how warming disrupts multiple metabolic processes simultaneously through coral loss.

## Coral as an Ecological Hub: Temperature Acts Through Structure

**Coral as an ecological hub: why temperature acts through structure rather than physiology**

The central finding of this analysis is that two decades of ocean warming have degraded reef ecosystem function primarily by dismantling coral structure, not by directly suppressing the physiology of individual organisms. Across every ecosystem variable we examined — respiration, photosynthesis, herbivory, corallivory, and nutrient cycling — the indirect temperature effect mediated through coral decline was either larger than, or the only credible component of, the total thermal signal. Direct temperature effects on ecosystem respiration (β = 0.22, 95% CI −0.21 to 0.62) and maximum photosynthetic capacity (β = −0.16, 95% CI −0.79 to 0.46) were both inconclusive, while their indirect counterparts (−0.58 and −0.19 respectively) were directionally credible. This pattern is not a statistical artefact: it reflects an ecological reality in which coral colonies function as keystone structures rather than just organisms. Coral provides physical framework, photosynthetic biomass, associated heterotrophic microbiomes, and three-dimensional habitat simultaneously; warming-induced bleaching and mortality therefore cascades across all of these pathways at once.

This contrasts sharply with the more commonly invoked direct warming hypothesis, in which ocean temperature is expected to stimulate microbial and heterotrophic metabolism (as in terrestrial systems) or suppress photosynthesis through bleaching of individual symbionts. Our data do not rule out those mechanisms acting at sub-annual timescales, but at the decadal scale of community reorganisation, structural loss appears to be the dominant transmission pathway. Ecosystem respiration declined 49% over 20 years not because metabolic rate constants fell, but because the coral-associated heterotrophic biomass that drives reef respiration — corals, their endosymbionts, and associated microbial communities — was removed. The mechanism is closer to deforestation than to metabolic inhibition.

## Ecosystem De-development and Metabolic Integration

The metabolic consequences of coral loss can be understood through Odum's (1969) concept of ecosystem development. Mature ecosystems are characterised by high biomass, low net production, high respiration, and tight internal cycling of nutrients — a configuration in which most fixed carbon is rapidly respired and recycled within the system rather than exported. Coral reefs are canonical examples of this functional type: extremely high gross production and respiration in oligotrophic water, sustained by tight coral-zooxanthellae-microbiome recycling. Our 20-year record documents a directional departure from this configuration. Both Pmax and Rd declined, but respiration showed a stronger and more consistent temporal signal (R² = 0.50 vs 0.19 for Pmax), and the SEM revealed that coral cover is a stronger predictor of respiration (β = 1.08) than of photosynthesis (β = −0.35, 95% CI crosses zero). The result is a gradual shift toward lower total metabolic activity rather than a simple shift in autotrophic–heterotrophic balance. In Odum's framework, this represents ecosystem retrogression: a trajectory from high-complexity, low-net-production towards lower biomass, lower respiratory capacity, and looser nutrient coupling.

The respiration–nitrogen pathway (β = 0.62, 95% CI 0.24–1.01) provides specific mechanistic support for this interpretation. Reduced ecosystem respiration — reflecting loss of coral-associated heterotrophic activity — correlates with lower algal tissue nitrogen content, consistent with reduced nutrient regeneration from organic matter decomposition in oligotrophic backreef water. Coral reefs are well known for efficient internal nitrogen cycling, and our data suggest that as the heterotrophic component of that cycle is reduced, nitrogen availability declines even for the macroalgae that are competitively replacing coral. This feedback — reduced respiration limiting the productivity of the organisms benefiting from coral decline — may partly explain why macroalgal expansion in oligotrophic Pacific reefs tends to be less extreme than on eutrophied Caribbean reefs.

## Indirect Effects Along Trophic Pathways

The two causal chains through community composition — Coral → Fleshy Algae → Herbivores, and Coral → Corallivores — show a coherent but ecologically nuanced response to warming. Corallivore fish biomass declined in parallel with coral cover (β = 0.65, 95% CI 0.25–1.04), as expected for a guild with obligate dietary dependence on live coral. Herbivore fish biomass, by contrast, increased over the same period (β_indirect temperature = +0.34, 95% CI 0.06–0.77), driven by expanding macroalgal food resources. At first glance this might seem compensatory, but the two responses operate through distinct pathways and the herbivore increase does not prevent macroalgal expansion — instead, the macroalgae–herbivore relationship represents bottom-up resource tracking rather than top-down regulation of algal abundance. Fleshy macroalgae expanded despite (and indeed facilitated) herbivore increases, suggesting that herbivory alone is insufficient to prevent phase-shift dynamics when coral structural complexity is lost.

These trophic dynamics have practical management implications. The consistent dominance of indirect (coral-mediated) over direct temperature effects across all six ecosystem variables implies that interventions targeting coral — whether through bleaching mitigation, shade structures, or active restoration — should in principle intercept the cascades before they propagate to fish assemblages, metabolism, and nutrient cycling. Local management of herbivore populations (e.g., controlling sea urchin or fish harvest) may be insufficient on its own if the primary leverage point is further upstream in the causal chain. Conversely, the fact that multiple ecosystem properties are coupled through a single hub suggests that successful coral recovery could trigger broad functional recovery, rather than requiring separate management of each endpoint.

## Comparison with Global Reef Trajectories

The MCR LTER Site 1 backreef trajectory is consistent with, but mechanistically more specific than, the global picture of reef decline. Widespread reductions in net community calcification (e.g., Albright et al. 2018; DeCarlo et al. 2017) and increasing heterotrophy (e.g., Kaneohe Bay; Shamberger et al. 2011) have been documented across ocean basins, but few studies have linked these to structural community change through an explicit causal framework. Our SEM results support a structural interpretation: metabolic decline tracks coral loss with a strong, credible path coefficient, whereas direct temperature effects are ambiguous. This suggests that the mechanistic driver of metabolic change at MCR is more closely analogous to the deforestation narrative than to the thermal inhibition narrative, with implications for projections: reef metabolism may recover if and when coral cover recovers, even if temperatures remain elevated.

The CMIP6 SSP scenario projections extend this finding forward in time. The 7-fold contrast in coral cover at 2100 between SSP1-2.6 (~6%) and SSP5-8.5 (~1%) illustrates the degree to which emission trajectory controls long-term reef outcomes — a result consistent with global projections of mass coral bleaching frequency under high-emissions scenarios (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2018; Hughes et al. 2017). Critically, the scenarios remain indistinguishable in their reef consequences until approximately 2040–2050, implying that the next two decades of warming are largely committed regardless of mitigation effort. The divergence thereafter, however, highlights that aggressive emissions reduction remains the most effective lever for preserving reef function at the centennial timescale. The SSP1-2.6 projection — in which MCR coral cover stabilises near its 2025 level rather than collapsing further — represents the ecosystem consequence of achieving the Paris Agreement ~1.5–2°C target and provides an ecologically grounded argument for that policy goal.

## Limitations and Future Directions

Several constraints bound the current analysis. First, this is a single-site study, and the path structure of the SEM reflects the particular ecological context of an oligotrophic Society Islands backreef. Whether the same causal architecture — and in particular the dominance of indirect temperature effects — holds at other sites with different nutrient regimes, disturbance histories, or species assemblages is an open empirical question. Second, the Bayesian SEM assumes linearity in all path coefficients on the z-score scale; potential nonlinearities, threshold behaviour, or lagged effects (e.g., multi-year bleaching recovery) are not captured. Third, the nutrient imputation model for water column chemistry (R² = 0.68) introduces uncertainty into the respiration–nitrogen pathway that is not fully propagated through the effect decomposition. Direct water column measurements, currently unavailable after 2018, would strengthen this component of the analysis.

Regarding the CMIP6 scenario projections specifically, three additional caveats apply. The coupled-model SST forcing is location-specific but at CMIP6 resolution (~1°), and cannot capture local oceanographic variability such as ENSO-driven anomalies, wave-driven upwelling, or fine-scale circulation around Moorea; the delta bias correction anchors the ensemble mean to the observed record but does not constrain interannual variance. The log-linear SEM extrapolates fleshy macroalgae beyond the 100% biological ceiling under SSP5-8.5, an artefact of model extrapolation beyond the observed range that should be interpreted qualitatively as indicating a phase-shifted, algae-dominated state. Finally, SEM path coefficients are assumed stationary across the projection window; adaptive responses by coral populations, non-linear bleaching thresholds, and potential acclimatisation dynamics are not represented.

Future directions include cross-site SEM comparison across MCR LTER sites (forereef, fringing reef, and backreef habitats differ substantially in hydrodynamics and community structure), experimental manipulation of herbivore density to test the causal role of the algae–herbivore pathway, and extension of the time series to capture post-bleaching dynamics in the late 2020s and to update projection baselines as the observational record grows.

## Box 1: Coral Reefs as Metabolic Paradigms — From Odum to Decline

**From healthy reefs to ecosystem dysfunction**: In 1954, Howard T. Odum conducted the first whole-ecosystem metabolism measurements at Eniwetok Atoll in the Marshall Islands, revolutionizing our understanding of coral reefs and ecosystem ecology broadly. Using innovative upstream-downstream oxygen flux techniques, Odum and colleagues demonstrated that coral reefs maintain exceptionally high gross production (200-400 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹), rivaling the most productive terrestrial ecosystems despite occurring in nutrient-poor tropical waters. Crucially, Odum showed that reef production and respiration were nearly balanced (P/R ≈ 1), indicating "mature" ecosystems maintaining high biomass with minimal net production—energy was tightly recycled rather than exported.

**Conceptual contributions**: Odum's reef studies established foundational concepts in ecosystem ecology: (1) **P/R ratios as maturity indices** - mature systems approach metabolic balance; (2) **Nutrient spiraling** - efficient nutrient retention and recycling in oligotrophic environments; (3) **Trophic efficiency** - high biomass per unit energy flow through tight food web linkages; (4) **Ecosystem development** - progression from r-selected, high-net-production systems to K-selected, high-biomass systems. Coral reefs became the archetype of "climax" ecosystems optimized for stability rather than growth.

**Contemporary decline**: Our MCR data reveal the reversal of Odum's trajectory. Where Eniwetok showed P/R ≈ 1 with high biomass and efficient nutrient cycling, MCR exhibits increasing P/R (from ~`r round(mean(Year_Averages$P_R_ratio[Year_Averages$Year %in% 2008:2010], na.rm = TRUE), 1)` to ~`r round(mean(Year_Averages$P_R_ratio[Year_Averages$Year %in% 2023:2025], na.rm = TRUE), 1)`) driven by collapsing biomass (70% coral loss) and disproportionate loss of respiratory capacity, alongside disrupted nutrient dynamics (respiration-N coupling weakened). This represents **ecosystem retrogression**—the undoing of ecological development. The shift away from P/R ≈ 1 reflects loss of the tight metabolic balance that characterized mature coral reefs, replaced by metabolic imbalance where production persists but respiratory biomass is lost. Climate change is dismantling the metabolic paradigm Odum described, with coral reefs losing the very characteristics that made them foundational to ecosystem science. The MCR time series documents this transition in unprecedented detail, providing a metabolic obituary for a disappearing ecosystem type.

## Box 2: Structural Equation Modelling for Causal Inference in Long-Term Ecology

**The challenge**: Long-term ecological monitoring generates rich observational data across multiple variables, but distinguishing correlation from causation remains difficult. Traditional regression approaches test pairwise relationships but cannot simultaneously evaluate complex networks of direct and indirect effects. This is critical for understanding how climate impacts cascade through ecosystems—does temperature affect fish biomass directly through physiological stress, or indirectly through coral habitat loss?

**Bayesian SEM solution**: Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) extends regression to multivariate systems with explicit causal structure. We specify hypothesized relationships among variables using a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), where arrows represent causal pathways (e.g., Temperature → Coral → Respiration). The Bayesian implementation offers key advantages: (1) **Uncertainty quantification** - full posterior distributions for all parameters, not just point estimates; (2) **Missing data handling** - imputation integrated into model estimation; (3) **Prior information** - incorporates ecological knowledge through weakly informative priors; (4) **Effect decomposition** - separates direct effects (Temperature → Respiration) from indirect effects (Temperature → Coral → Respiration) using posterior sampling.

**Application to MCR**: Our DAG encoded eight causal relationships based on ecological theory (e.g., coral loss causes algal expansion; algae support herbivores) and temporal precedence (temperature drives coral loss, not vice versa). The Bayesian SEM revealed that **indirect effects dominate** for metabolic variables—temperature impacts respiration 2-3× more strongly through coral decline than through direct thermal effects. This finding was invisible to pairwise correlations but emerged from the full causal network.

**Broader implications**: The approach is applicable to any long-term monitoring program with multivariate data and hypothesized causal structure. LTER sites, marine observatories, and climate monitoring networks all collect data suitable for SEM, yet most analyses remain correlative. Our workflow (DAG specification → Bayesian estimation → effect decomposition → projection) provides a template for extracting causal insights from observational time series, advancing LTER from description to mechanistic understanding. The key is being explicit about causal assumptions (DAG) rather than pretending they don't exist in correlation analysis.

# Supplementary Material

## Supplementary Figure 1: Photosynthesis-Irradiance Curves

```{r fig-pi-curves}
#| label: fig-pi-curves
#| fig-cap: "**Supplementary Figure 1. Annual photosynthesis-irradiance (PI) curves for MCR LTER Site 1 backreef, 2008–2025.** Points show individual hourly net community production measurements (mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹) plotted against photosynthetically active radiation (PAR; µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹). Lines show the fitted rectangular hyperbola for each year, with parameters (α, Pmax, Rd) estimated simultaneously from all 2,928 observations using the Bayesian non-linear model described in Methods. Inset text in each panel shows the posterior median Pmax and Rd (rounded to the nearest integer; units: mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹). The progressive decline in both Pmax and Rd across years reflects the loss of photosynthetic capacity and ecosystem respiration documented in the main text."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

par_seq <- seq(0, max(LTER1_Pnet$PAR, na.rm = TRUE), length.out = 200)

pi_params_plot <- fixef(fit1_f) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("param") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  separate(param, into = c("type", "year_str"), sep = "_Year", remove = FALSE) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(year_str)) |>
  filter(!is.na(year)) |>
  select(type, year, Estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = Estimate) |>
  mutate(Rd = -Rd)

fitted_curves <- pi_params_plot |>
  rowwise() |>
  reframe(
    year   = year,
    PAR    = par_seq,
    PP_fit = (alpha * Pmax * par_seq) / (alpha * par_seq + Pmax) - Rd
  )

raw_data_plot <- LTER1_Pnet |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(as.character(Year)))

param_labels <- pi_params_plot |>
  mutate(
    label = sprintf("Pmax = %.0f\nRd = %.0f", Pmax, Rd),
    PAR   = max(LTER1_Pnet$PAR, na.rm = TRUE) * 0.97,
    PP    = min(LTER1_Pnet$PP,  na.rm = TRUE) * 0.85
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = raw_data_plot,
             aes(x = PAR, y = PP),
             colour = "grey50", size = 0.5, alpha = 0.4, shape = 16) +
  geom_line(data = fitted_curves,
            aes(x = PAR, y = PP_fit),
            colour = "#1A237E", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_text(data = param_labels,
            aes(x = PAR, y = PP, label = label),
            hjust = 1, vjust = 0, size = 2.2, colour = "#1A237E",
            lineheight = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol = 6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1000, 2000)) +
  labs(
    x = expression(PAR~(mu*mol~photons~m^{-2}~s^{-1})),
    y = expression(Net~production~(mmol~O[2]~m^{-2}~hr^{-1}))
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    strip.text       = element_text(size = 7.5, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text        = element_text(size = 6)
  )
```

## Supplementary Table 1: SEM Path Coefficients

```{r tbl-sem-paths}
#| label: tbl-sem-paths
#| tbl-cap: "**Supplementary Table 1.** Standardised path coefficients from the Bayesian multivariate structural equation model (12 pathways, n = 20 annual observations, 2005–2025). All continuous variables were log-transformed where appropriate and z-score standardised (mean = 0, SD = 1) prior to modelling. Year residual is the residual of calendar year regressed on maximum annual temperature, capturing secular coral decline beyond the thermal trend. β = posterior median standardised path coefficient; 95% CI = posterior credible interval; Rhat = potential scale reduction factor (values < 1.01 indicate convergence); Bulk ESS = bulk effective sample size; Tail ESS = tail effective sample size. Pathways for which the 95% CI excludes zero are considered credible (marked †)."

# Build tidy table from brms fixed effects summary
sem_coef_table <- as.data.frame(summary(brms_sem_full)$fixed) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
  # Keep only regression coefficients (exclude intercepts)
  filter(!grepl("Intercept", term)) |>
  mutate(
    # Parse response and predictor from "response_predictor" format
    Pathway = case_when(
      term == "temperature_Year"         ~ "Year → Temperature",
      term == "logcoral_temperature"     ~ "Temperature → Coral cover",
      term == "logcoral_yearresid"       ~ "Year residual → Coral cover",
      term == "logrd_logcoral"           ~ "Coral cover → Ecosystem respiration",
      term == "logrd_mitemperature"      ~ "Temperature → Ecosystem respiration (direct)",
      term == "logfleshy_logcoral"       ~ "Coral cover → Fleshy macroalgae",
      term == "Corallivore_logcoral"     ~ "Coral cover → Corallivore biomass",
      term == "herbs_logfleshy"          ~ "Fleshy macroalgae → Herbivore biomass",
      term == "logpmax_milogrd"          ~ "Ecosystem respiration → Ecosystem Pmax",
      term == "logpmax_logcoral"         ~ "Coral cover → Ecosystem Pmax (direct)",
      term == "logpmax_mitemperature"    ~ "Temperature → Ecosystem Pmax (direct)",
      term == "Npercent_milogrd"         ~ "Ecosystem respiration → Algal N content",
      TRUE ~ term
    ),
    Credible = if_else(sign(`l-95% CI`) == sign(`u-95% CI`), "†", ""),
    beta  = sprintf("%.3f", Estimate),
    CI    = sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", `l-95% CI`, `u-95% CI`),
    Rhat  = sprintf("%.4f", Rhat),
    BESS  = formatC(round(Bulk_ESS), format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    TESS  = formatC(round(Tail_ESS), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
  ) |>
  # Order by causal chain
  mutate(order = case_when(
    grepl("Year →",              Pathway) ~ 1,
    grepl("Temperature →",       Pathway) ~ 2,
    grepl("Year residual →",     Pathway) ~ 2,
    grepl("Coral cover →",       Pathway) ~ 3,
    grepl("Fleshy macroalgae →", Pathway) ~ 4,
    grepl("Ecosystem respiration →", Pathway) ~ 5,
    TRUE ~ 6
  )) |>
  arrange(order, Pathway) |>
  select(Pathway, Credible, beta, CI, Rhat, `Bulk ESS` = BESS, `Tail ESS` = TESS)

kable(sem_coef_table, align = c("l", "c", "r", "c", "r", "r", "r"),
      col.names = c("Pathway", "", "β", "95% CI", "R̂", "Bulk ESS", "Tail ESS")) |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE,
                font_size = 12) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "14em") |>
  column_spec(2, width = "1em") |>
  footnote(symbol = "95% credible interval excludes zero.")
```

# Conclusions

This long-term analysis of Moorea's backreef ecosystem demonstrates the value of integrated, multi-decadal monitoring for understanding reef dynamics. The data reveal:

1.  **Clear directional change** in community composition driven primarily by warming
2.  **Complex feedbacks** among benthic communities, fish assemblages, and biogeochemical processes
3.  **Declining ecosystem function** as measured by net productivity and respiratory capacity
4.  **Predictable trajectories** that can inform management and restoration planning

Future research should focus on:

-   Identifying potential thresholds and tipping points in the transition process
-   Understanding resilience mechanisms and recovery potential
-   Evaluating management interventions to alter current trajectories
-   Exploring fine-scale spatial heterogeneity in ecosystem responses

The structural equation modeling approach employed here provides a framework for testing causal hypotheses and making projections, but predictions should be interpreted cautiously given the complexity of reef systems and potential for non-linear dynamics.
